The technique exists because context is a cost twice over. Every

stuffed with the full style guide, deployment runbook, and database conventions makes the agent worse at all of them — the instructions that matter for the current task are diluted by the ones that don't. The tell is an agent that ignores rules you know are in its context: they're in there, but buried.

Progressive disclosure inverts this. Keep the always-loaded layer small — a sentence per topic and a pointer to where the detail lives. The agent reads the style guide when it's writing a component, the deployment runbook when it's deploying, and neither when it's fixing a test.

"Should I dump the entire style guide into AGENTS.md?"
"No — progressive disclosure. Reference the style guide as a skill the agent loads when it actually needs to write a component. AGENTS.md pays the token cost every turn."
